title: Positive-dimensional finitely generated domains have infinitely many maximal ideals
statement: Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a finitely generated $k$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] that is an integral domain (a commutative ring with no zero divisors). If the Krull dimension of $A$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] is positive, then $A$ has infinitely many maximal ideals.

source.place: the affine positive-dimension argument used with Tags 00G1 and 00FV: a finite-type domain with only finitely many maximal ideals is zero-dimensional

proof.text: Assume for contradiction that the set M of maximal ideals of A is finite. By lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-field-prime-intersection-maximal, A is Jacobson. Since A is a domain, the zero ideal is prime, so its Jacobson radical equals zero. Every ideal contains zero, hence the finite infimum of all members of M equals zero.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma 00G1 (algebra-lemma-finite-type-field-Jacobson) and Theorem 00FV (algebra-theorem-nullstellensatz), affine positive-dimension argument

proof.text: A finite infimum of ideals that is prime equals one of its factors (Mathlib Ideal.eq_inf_of_isPrime_inf, proved using the product of the ideals and primality). Apply this to the finite family M whose infimum is zero. Thus a member of M is zero, so zero is maximal and A is a field (Ring.isField_iff_maximal_bot). The finite-infimum lemma also rules out an empty M, without a separate maximal-ideal existence argument.
The spectrum of a field has only the zero prime ideal, so it has no nontrivial strict chain of prime ideals and its Krull dimension is zero.
This contradicts the hypothesis that the Krull dimension of A is positive. Hence the maximal ideals of A are not finite in number, and therefore A has infinitely many maximal ideals.
